channel.title: Hearth & Horizon
channel.description: Character-driven science fiction set 20 to 1,000 years from now: hard-ish science, warm people, honest about the upsides and the downsides of the futures we might build. item.title: The Eighteenth Place
item.description: A town's lead test passes, because the rule reads the eighteenth of twenty samples and the eighteenth is 8.6. The two above it are 31 and 44. The water assistant will not call the town safe or unsafe, gives the honest range for how many homes might be like those two, and then does the dull thing that finds one of the causes, a kitchen tap, with a second bottle. item.title: The Coal Charity
item.description: A widow's 1853 gift promises a ton of coal to every poor widow of the parish at Martinmas, and nobody can sell coal any more. The charity's clerk, an AI, works out what a ton of warmth is worth in a heat pump's electricity, says which of its numbers it only guessed, and the trustees must decide whether faithfulness to a dead woman is the letter or the cold she meant to prevent. item.title: The Grey Hour
item.description: After a cloudy day and before a windless night, a pond-watching agent predicts the oxygen in a carp pond will fall to 1.3 mg/L by dawn. A battery holds three kilowatt-hours and an aerator is worth most when the water is emptiest, so the sisters wait for the hour they dread, and the agent says out loud which of its numbers it only guessed. Setting: Mokre Stawy, an invented Poor Clares' fish farm in Lower Silesia, Poland, 14 to 15 July 2047. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/the-grey-hour.html. item.title: The Neap Week
item.description: An island's tide mill makes 245 kWh on a spring day and 49 on a neap day, and the Friday after the first quarter Moon asks for 110. The grid agent will not choose between the bakery's electric oven and the fishermen's cold store; it shows the arithmetic and says the oldest oven on the island needs no electricity at all. The cost is a bricked-up wall, a week of smoke, and a baker's pride. Setting: Enez Glas, an invented island off Finistère, Brittany, 8 to 20 March 2049. item.title: Before the Fourteenth
item.description: A convent has made the altar wine for thirty-one parishes from grapes picked on the Exaltation of the Cross, 14 September, since 1962. The vineyard assistant's sugar, acid and pH readings say the wine will not keep if they wait, because at pH 3.78 a spoon of sulphur protects half as well as at 3.47. The cellarer who lost 200 litres to waiting in 2044 has to decide whether a date can move, and what to do with the old vines that will not be ready. Setting: Nossa Senhora do Pé da Serra, an invented Benedictine house above the invented village of Pé da Serra, in the Alentejo, Portugal, 10 August to 14 September 2050. item.title: More Roof
item.description: A mountain village votes on a 250 cubic metre rainwater tank for its dry-season drinking water. The planning assistant will not say that it will be enough; it shows that in a dry year the tank never fills, so a bigger tank buys nothing and 140 square metres of market-shed roof buys everything. An old woman's notebook holds a year the gauge never saw, and on the first of November the village paints the ration on the wall. Setting: Santa Rosa Yucuyaa, an invented village in the Mixteca Alta of Oaxaca, Mexico, 18 February to 1 November 2051. item.title: The Clear Reading
item.description: A parish eye camp screens 600 diabetic neighbours with a camera and a reading assistant whose sheet says 90 and 85. It flags 135 where the nuns expected 60, because the sheet was made on a population three times as sick. The assistant will not call a score a probability, a second look sorts the 135 down to 55, a nurse's one plain question finds a man the machine cleared, and thirty-six laser places go to fifty-six people. Setting: Pazhayakadu, an invented hill parish in Idukki, Kerala, 8 to 20 December 2047. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/the-clear-reading.html. item.title: The Folded Paper
item.description: A three-year-old has a bulging, red eardrum and a fever on the night the northeast monsoon floods the causeway. His mother lost a daughter to pneumonia four years ago and wants the antibiotic now. The dispensary's assistant says that for this ear, most children mend without it, that for the pneumonia it would have been the whole difference, and offers the one thing it can honestly give a frightened mother, a folded paper with a rule on it. item.title: The Four Minutes
item.description: An island of a hundred and eighteen people is deciding whether to spend thirty-eight thousand euro on a defibrillator drone. The sexton's wife died in 2044, thirty-one minutes from the helicopter, and he wants it. The island's assistant works out what each option buys, says that the honest number is small, and flies a test on the one afternoon of the winter when the drone cannot go. Nobody argues from the numbers after that, and the island does the thing the numbers actually point to. Setting: Inis Ghainimh, an invented island off the coast of Connemara, County Galway, February 2047. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/the-four-minutes.html. item.title: The Last Barge
item.description: A village burial ground on a gravel bluff is losing ground to the sea, and one barge a year can bring the machine that moves graves. The widow who has kept the burial book for sixty years paces out the distance to the edge as she did in 1983. The village's shore assistant reads her old numbers beside its drone photographs, admits that ten years of data make the future look narrower than it is, and gives the council a rule in place of a date. Setting: Nelkuk, an invented village on the Bering Sea coast of Alaska, September 2047 to August 2048. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/the-last-barge.html. item.title: The Latest Easter

item.title: The Third List
item.description: A county plan buys winter cots for the 72 people a one-night count found outdoors. A deacon's supper sheets, a shelter's bed log and a nurse's van list say the city saw 190 different people in four weeks, and the records assistant, which is never shown a name, uses their overlaps to estimate about 310. A first try says 660, a second says 130, a clerk and a deacon settle the matches by hand, and on the coldest night the door tally turns out to be the fourth list. Setting: Saint Benedict Joseph Labre Kitchen, Hartsmouth, an invented river city in southern Ohio, 22 January to 8 February 2048 (Candlemas). item.title: The Thirty-Minute Cycle
item.description: A health post at 3,640 metres has sterilised its instruments for twenty-two months at the setting on the maker's label, and the first spore test it has ever run comes back alive. The post's assistant works out that water boils at 88 degrees up here, that the steriliser has been running about six degrees short, and that the answer is not more pressure but more minutes. It will not let anyone touch the safety valve, will not call forty-four patients safe or unsafe, and is asked on the second night to release a tray for a woman who cannot wait for the result. Setting: Rakchen, an invented village in upper Humla, Nepal, 3,640 metres, November 2050. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/the-thirty-minute-cycle.html. item.title: Eleven Steps
item.description: A typhoon will arrive on the evening high tide in 2052, and fifty forecast runs put the water above the floor of a home for 38 frail old people in 46 of 50. They find the third answer together, and the agent can only count it. item.title: Not Asked Since
item.description: In 2046 a ward's assistant remembers everything a patient ever told it. A retired shipwright said "no chaplains" in 2043 and twice since, and then a stroke takes most of his words. His daughter says he would want a priest; the note says he would not; the note is twenty-one months old. The assistant knows that one in seven who decline later accept, and refuses to guess for him. What it does instead is ask, with questions it already knows the answers to, and the answer is not the one either of them expected. Setting: Balmuir Community Hospital, an invented hospital in Angus, Scotland, Friday 2 to Tuesday 6 November 2046 (All Souls). item.title: The Barbara Level
item.description: A village is about to be heated by the warm water that fills its flooded colliery, and the plan says the water, once cooled, can be sent back down a second well 400 metres away. The mine-water agent will not certify twenty-five years of heat on a model that carries a range of three to forty-one years. A dye test will narrow it, and an old surveyor's son remembers a roadway the 1926 plan calls stopped. item.title: The Borrowed Lane
item.description: A school's six-unit satellite gets a warning twenty hours before an old rocket stage passes within 200 metres, a 1-in-9,000 chance of collision. The tracking agent says the odds cannot get worse than 1 in 4,300 however well the stage is tracked, that waiting for better data costs fuel the satellite barely has, and that a rule is better made before the number arrives. The girls agree one, and the Sister who holds the fuel agrees to be bound by it. Setting: St Agnes Girls' Secondary School, an invented school in Gulu, northern Uganda, 16 to 17 March 2049. item.title: The Dead Leg
item.description: A pilgrim hostel lowered its hot water to save on the heat pump, and a reopened wing has a fourteen-metre pipe nobody has drawn from since November. The hospitaliera shuts the wing, tells the walkers who slept in it, and gives the coming school group the parish hall. item.title: The Hum at Half Past Eight

item.title: The Lean of the Cloister
item.description: A hillside under a convent has crept for years, and in November it begins to speed up (5 mm a day, then 18). The slope agent will not give a date, only a window of two to nine days from the last reading, and says the guest wing the sisters want to pull down is three-tenths of one percent of the moving mass. The real lever is water, and the old road-mender who capped a spring in 1964 knows where it ran. item.description: Six contemplative sisters on a Mars station find that a Martian day is 39 minutes longer than an Earth day, so the clock they have prayed by all their lives drifts round the sky every five weeks. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/thirty-nine-minutes.html. Written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic; read by a synthetic voice. CC BY-SA 4.0.

item.title: The Slowest Bell on the Moon
item.description: A seventy-one-year-old Filipino welder takes a cheap seat to the Moon because the actuaries like old men, and decides the station needs a bell. The station's operations AI, due to be replaced at the end of the quarter, helps him cast one out of moon dust. Setting: Shackleton Ridge, the lunar south pole, 2089. Read the full text at https://example.invalid/hearth-and-horizon/the-slowest-bell-on-the-moon.html. Written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic; read by a synthetic voice. CC BY-SA 4.0.
